What the official sources say

  • To get an assessor hearing between June 15 and July 5, the owner must file a protest with the assessor; mailed protests are timely if postmarked by June 30. (Protests and Appeals | DPT; source)
  • An appeal to the County Board of Equalization (CBOE) must be postmarked or made in person no later than July 20. (Protests and Appeals | DPT; source)
  • The CBOE must conclude hearings and render value decisions on or before August 5 and mail its determination within five business days of the decision. (Protests and Appeals | DPT; source)
  • After a CBOE decision, the taxpayer may appeal to the Board of Assessment Appeals (BAA), use binding arbitration, or go to district court. (Protests and Appeals | DPT; source)
  • 2026 residential assessment rates are 6.8% (local government) and 7.05% (school districts). (Understanding Property Taxes in Colorado | DPT; source)
  • Real property Notices of Valuation are mailed by May 1 each year. (Understanding Property Taxes in Colorado | DPT; source)
  • Colorado sells tax liens (not deeds) at an annual county tax lien sale; Weld County's next sale is November 5, 2026, held online. (Tax Lien Sale Information | Weld County; source)
  • The property owner may redeem from the certificate holder any time after the sale up to issuance of a Treasurer's Deed. (Tax Lien Sale Information | Weld County; source)

How is Colorado property tax calculated?

Colorado property tax is the assessed value of a property multiplied by the combined mill levies of every taxing authority that covers it. The Division of Property Taxation explains that the assessor estimates actual value, a classification-based assessment rate turns that into assessed value, and each taxing body then applies its own tax rate.

Its worked example uses a $275,000 home. Local government levies of 0.023425 on $18,700 of assessed value come to $438.05, school district levies of 0.052116 on $19,388 come to $1,010.43, and the total is $1,448.48. A mill is one tenth of a cent, so 13.980 mills is written as 0.013980.

Property is classified by how it is used on January 1. Residential property is valued only with the market approach, meaning comparable sales, while most commercial and personal property can also be valued by cost and income.

Who sets what: assessor, taxing districts and treasurer?

Different offices handle valuation, rates and collection, which is why a Colorado seller may need to call more than one number. The state's property tax pages divide the roles this way.

  • County assessor: finds, classifies and values all property, mails valuation notices and decides protests.
  • Taxing authorities: county commissioners, city councils, school boards and special district boards decide how much revenue they need and set their rates.
  • County board of equalization: hears appeals from assessor decisions.
  • Arbitrators, district court or the Board of Assessment Appeals: hear appeals from the county board.
  • County treasurer: sends the bill and collects. El Paso County's Treasurer says statements go to the owner of record on the tax roll, and not getting one does not excuse a late payment.

Colorado has 64 counties, so there are 64 assessors and treasurers, and Denver and Broomfield combine city and county government. Always check the county where the house sits.

What are the 2026 assessment rates by property type?

For 2026 the state sets different rates for each class, and residential property gets the lowest. Residential is 6.8% for local government levies and 7.05% for school districts, according to the Division of Property Taxation.

Classification (2026)Assessment rate
Residential, local government6.8%
Residential, schools7.05%
Vacant land26%
Commercial improved25%
Commercial other26%
Industrial26%
Agricultural25%
State assessed26%

A seller with a vacant lot or a rental that is classed as commercial should look at the notice of valuation for the class the assessor assigned. The class drives the rate, so a misclassified parcel can raise the bill.

When does Colorado reassess property?

Real property is revalued every odd-numbered year, and personal property every year. The assessor mails real property notices of valuation by May 1.

For tax years 2025 and 2026, residential values rest on sales from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024, and the state allows earlier six-month windows when data is thin. El Paso County's Assessor describes 2025 values as applying to tax year 2026 with a 2023 base year. In even-numbered years, that office says only properties with a change receive a notice.

That lag affects sellers. A buyer's bill follows the assessor's value, not the contract price, so a sale well above or below the assessor's figure does not rewrite the bill until the next reappraisal.

When are Colorado property taxes due?

Colorado bills go out as soon after January 1 as possible, and the owner can pay in full by April 30 or in two halves. Taxes of $25 or less are due in full by April 30, while larger bills can be split into a payment due the last day of February and a second due June 15.

The county treasurer enforces the dates. El Paso County reports interest of 1% per month on late payments with no grace period and no partial payments, and says taxes unpaid after June 15 become delinquent. It adds that after September 30, payments must be in cash or certified funds, and personal checks and postmarks are not accepted.

Colorado collects overdue real estate tax through a tax lien sale rather than a tax deed sale. El Paso County's 2026 sale is scheduled for October 28, 2026, run electronically through RealAuction, with registration opening September 30, 2026. Ask the county treasurer how long the redemption period runs after a sale.

How do I appeal a Colorado property tax assessment?

You start with the county assessor, then move to the county board of equalization, and from there to the Board of Assessment Appeals, district court or binding arbitration. El Paso County is a useful example because it publishes its calendar.

  • El Paso Assessor: the formal appeal period runs from May 1 to June 8, and the office answers with a Notice of Determination by August 15.
  • El Paso Board of Equalization: for 2026 the real property protest date is July 15, and hearings run July 6 through August 5, held by Teams.
  • Hearing format: each side gets 10 minutes, and the petitioner carries the burden of proving value.
  • Decision: the written decision arrives within five business days of the hearing.
  • Next steps: an appeal of the board's decision must be filed within 30 days of the postmark.

Evidence is limited to market data from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024 for the 2025 and 2026 values. Repair estimates, an independent appraisal and photos of conditions that lower value are all listed as acceptable. Other counties use different forms and dates, so confirm yours on the assessor's notice.

Which exemptions and deferrals can lower or delay a Colorado bill?

The main programs are the senior and disabled veteran exemptions, and the senior deferral. The senior exemption removes 50% of the first $200,000 of actual value of a primary residence, subject to state funding. The Division of Property Taxation lists it for owners age 65 or older who owned and occupied the home for at least 10 consecutive years, with a July 15 filing date at the assessor.

  • Veteran with a disability and Gold Star spouse: the same 50% of the first $200,000, filed by July 1.
  • Qualified senior primary residence classification: for tax years 2025 and 2026, for former exemption holders who moved, filed by March 15.
  • Senior deferral: age 65 or older, applied for between January 1 and April 1 with the county treasurer, renewed each year.

A deferral is a loan from the state treasurer that is recorded as a lien. The Division says repayment is required when the property is sold or title is transferred, and also on death, on moving for reasons other than health, or when the property is rented. Sellers with a deferral should request a payoff before closing.

Why do two Colorado homes of equal value get different bills?

Each home sits in its own combination of districts, and the levies differ widely. The El Paso County Treasurer's published table for tax year 2025, billed in 2026, shows how far apart they run.

El Paso County taxing entityMills, tax year 2025
El Paso County6.857
City of Colorado Springs3.009
Pikes Peak Library District2.938
Colorado Springs School District 1137.695
Academy School District 2045.459
Widefield School District 357.682

A house in one school district and a fire district can have a different total from a house a few miles away, and metro districts in newer subdivisions add more. Read the tax statement for the entities listed on the actual parcel.

What should a Colorado seller know about taxes at closing?

Ask the title company for the current year's status before you sign. The treasurer bills the owner of record, and a mortgage servicer may or may not hold taxes in escrow, so the owner should confirm with the lender, as El Paso County advises.

Hail and wildfire can also change what a house is worth to a buyer. Wikipedia's Colorado entry notes that hail is common east of the Continental Divide and that the May 8, 2017 Denver hailstorm was the costliest in state history, while the Marshall Fire of 2021 caused the most property loss of any Colorado wildfire. Sellers with unpaid tax and a damaged roof can ask for an as-is cash offer rather than funding repairs first.

What is the Colorado property tax due date?

Taxes are due April 30 in full, or in two halves due the last day of February and June 15. Bills of $25 or less are due in full by April 30, per the Division of Property Taxation.

How often does Colorado reassess property?

Every odd-numbered year for real property, with notices of valuation mailed by May 1. Personal property is revalued every year.

What interest applies to late Colorado property tax?

It depends on the county. El Paso County's Treasurer reports 1% per month with no grace period, and unpaid taxes are delinquent after June 15.

Can I get a property tax break as a Colorado senior?

Possibly. The state senior exemption covers 50% of the first $200,000 of actual value for owners 65 or older who have owned and lived in the home at least 10 consecutive years, depending on state funding. The application goes to the county assessor by July 15.

What happens to a senior tax deferral when I sell?

Repayment is required when the property is sold or title is transferred. The deferred taxes and interest are a lien, so they are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.

What the official sources say

  • Seniors 65+ who have owned and occupied their primary residence for at least 10 consecutive years before Jan. 1 of the application year may qualify for the Senior Property Tax Exemption. (Senior Property Tax Exemption | DPT; source)
  • The program exempts up to 50% of the first $200,000 of the home's actual value. (Senior Property Tax Exemption | DPT; source)
  • The application period each year runs from January 1 to July 15. (Senior Property Tax Exemption | DPT; source)

What does the Colorado homestead exemption protect?

The Colorado homestead exemption shields part of the equity in your home from creditors who hold a court judgment. It is separate from the property tax breaks for seniors, and the two get mixed up often.

Under C.R.S. 38-41-201, a homestead is exempt from execution and attachment for debts, contracts and civil obligations, up to a set amount of actual cash value above any liens in place when a levy happens. The protected amounts are:

Who occupies the homeProtected amount
An owner or the owner's family$250,000
An owner, spouse or dependent who is elderly or disabled$350,000

The statute defines elderly as age sixty or older. Disabled means a physical or mental impairment that substantially keeps the person from useful work in any job that exists in the community and fits their competence. The text we read is the 2024 edition as published by the Colorado legislature and mirrored on a public statute site, so confirm the figures against the current edition before you rely on them.

Do I have to file anything to claim it?

Usually no. Section 38-41-202 says the exemption is deemed created and can be claimed when the home is occupied and the property is the right kind of homestead.

There is a catch for debts older than a certain date. The statute says the exemption cannot be claimed against an obligation incurred before July 1, 1975, unless the owner recorded a written homestead statement with the county clerk and recorder. That date makes it a niche rule today.

A recorded statement still matters in one way. When an owner or spouse records the instrument, both spouses must sign to convey or encumber the property. Without a recording, a homestead that arises automatically can be conveyed or encumbered by the owner alone, with no other signature needed.

For a seller, that gives a clear checklist:

  • Search the county records for a recorded homestead declaration.
  • If one exists, plan for both spouses to sign the deed.
  • If none exists, only the owner of record needs to sign.

Does the home have to be lived in?

Yes. Section 38-41-203 says the property is exempt only while it is occupied as a home by the owner or the owner's family.

That rule affects houses people are about to sell. A house that has sat empty after a move, or one that is rented out, may no longer qualify for the protection. If a judgment creditor is in the picture, the date you moved out can matter.

The statute does not use the words vacant or rental, so a lawyer should read the facts before anyone relies on the exemption. For tenant-occupied properties, the eviction and landlord rules are the better starting point.

What happens when a creditor tries to force a sale of a homestead?

A creditor has to clear several hurdles first. Under C.R.S. 38-41-206, the creditor must file an affidavit with the county clerk and recorder and with the sheriff or other officer who would levy.

  • A description of the homestead and the name of the claimant.
  • The fair market value of the property.
  • A statement that value minus prior liens is above the exemption amount the claimant qualifies for.
  • A statement that no earlier execution from the same judgment has been levied.
  • A second affidavit from a professionally qualified independent appraiser with the same value information.

If the winning bid at the sale does not exceed seventy percent of the appraiser's fair market value, the proceedings end. The officer records a release of all levies, the person who started the case pays the costs, and the owner's title is not harmed.

If a sale does go through, the money is paid out in a fixed order:

  1. Prior liens and encumbrances.
  2. The homestead claimant, up to the exemption amount.
  3. Costs and expenses of the sale.
  4. The judgment.
  5. Anything left over, back to the claimant.

A judgment creditor who is the winning bidder must pay cash for the exemption plus costs, and cannot apply the exempt amount against the judgment.

Are the sale proceeds protected if I sell the house?

For a limited time, yes. C.R.S. 38-41-207 exempts the proceeds from execution or attachment for three years after you receive them, provided you keep the money separate so it can always be identified.

That covers the exempt amount when the owner sells the property, proceeds of a sale under section 38-41-206, and insurance money for destroyed homestead property held to restore or replace it.

There is also a carryover. If you use the proceeds to buy another home, the same exemption you had on the old house applies to the new one. It does not work against a vendor's lien or the holder of a purchase money mortgage on the new property.

The practical tip is simple. If you are selling a house while a creditor is pressing, do not mix the sale check into a general account. A separate account keeps the money traceable, which is what the statute asks for.

How is this different from the senior property tax exemption?

The homestead exemption is a creditor shield. The senior property tax exemption lowers a tax bill. They sit in different parts of the law and are run by different offices.

The Division of Property Taxation describes the senior exemption on its program notice and says each county accepts applications on a yearly cycle, with the application window opening January 1. County assessors take the applications.

The age, ownership and occupancy tests and the exempt share of value are set out in the state program summary higher on this page. Ask your county assessor for the current year's form.

If you plan to sell during the year, ask the county assessor how a sale affects an application already filed.

How do property taxes get paid when a Colorado house is sold?

Colorado lets the taxpayer pay the bill in full or in two installments, and section 39-10-104.5 sets the schedule. Any split between buyer and seller is a term of the sale contract.

OptionDue date
Pay in fullOn or before April 30, with no interest through that date
First halfLast day of February
Second halfJune 15

Interest runs at one percent per month once a payment is late. The statute says no installments are allowed on a total under $25, which must be paid in full by April 30. You can read the rule on the statute page.

Confirm the balance and any delinquent interest with the county treasurer before you set a closing date.

What does the county charge to record the deed?

Besides ordinary recording fees, a deed filed with the county clerk and recorder carries a documentary fee. Under C.R.S. 39-13-102 it is one cent for each $100 of consideration, and no fee applies when the consideration is $500 or less.

The person who offers the deed for recording pays it. For a $400,000 sale that works out to $40, using the one-cent rate as written in the statute.

If you are selling a house with a judgment or lien attached, we are glad to walk through the numbers with you, and we suggest a Colorado attorney for the legal questions.

More questions about Colorado Homestead Exemption

How much does the Colorado homestead exemption protect?

$250,000 for a home occupied by an owner or the owner's family, and $350,000 when the occupant is an elderly or disabled owner, spouse or dependent. Elderly means sixty or older under the statute.

Do I need to record a homestead declaration?

No. The exemption arises automatically if the occupancy and property-type rules are met. Recording a statement is only needed for older debts and changes who must sign a deed.

Does the homestead exemption stop me from selling my house?

No. It limits what a judgment creditor can collect from the home. It does not block a voluntary sale. A recorded declaration means both spouses must sign the deed.

How long are the sale proceeds protected?

Three years after you receive them, if you keep them separate and identifiable. If you buy another home with the money, the same exemption carries over to it.

Can a creditor force the sale of my home for any price?

No. If the winning bid is seventy percent or less of the appraised fair market value in the creditor's appraiser affidavit, the proceedings end and the creditor pays the costs.

When are Colorado property taxes due?

In full by April 30, or in two halves, the last day of February and June 15. Interest runs at one percent per month on late payments.

What is the documentary fee on a Colorado deed?

One cent for each $100 of consideration, collected by the county clerk and recorder, with no fee when the consideration is $500 or less.

What the official sources say

  • Colorado's estate tax equaled the federal state death tax credit, which was eliminated, effectively ending the Colorado estate tax for deaths after December 31, 2004. (Estate Tax | Colorado General Assembly; source)
  • Under current law, no Colorado estate tax filing is required for estates of individuals who die after December 31, 2004. (Estate Tax | Colorado General Assembly; source)
  • A state inheritance tax was enacted in 1927 and replaced by an estate tax in 1980. (Estate Tax | Colorado General Assembly; source)

Does Colorado have an estate tax or inheritance tax today?

No. Colorado collects neither on deaths after December 31, 2004. The Legislative Council Staff's estate tax handbook says the state estate tax was effectively eliminated for those deaths, and that under current law no Colorado estate tax filing is required.

The handbook adds that Colorado has not collected any estate taxes since fiscal year 2013-14. For a family selling an inherited house, that means the question is usually federal, not state.

Form DR 1210 is the exception: it applies only if the date of death was before December 31, 2004, according to the same handbook.

How did Colorado end up without the tax?

The state tax was tied to a federal credit, and when the credit disappeared so did the tax. A state inheritance tax was enacted in 1927. In 1980 the legislature replaced it with an estate tax.

That estate tax equaled the federal "state death tax credit" allowed on federal estate tax returns until 2005. Federal changes reduced the credit between 2002 and 2004 and then eliminated it. The handbook notes that if federal law ever reinstated the credit, a Colorado estate tax could be collected in future years.

Year or periodWhat happened
1927State inheritance tax enacted
1980Legislature replaced it with an estate tax
2002 to 2004Federal law reduced then ended the state death tax credit
After December 31, 2004No Colorado estate tax filing required
Since fiscal year 2013-14No estate tax revenue collected

What federal estate tax rules affect heirs in Colorado?

Only large estates owe federal estate tax, and filing depends on a yearly threshold. The IRS estate tax page lists the filing threshold for the year of death:

Year of deathReturn required above
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

The threshold counts the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption. The IRS says most simple estates do not need to file. Deductions are allowed for mortgages and other debts, administration expenses, and property that passes to a surviving spouse or qualified charities. A surviving spouse can also be given the decedent's unused exemption through an election on a timely return.

The estate counts everything at fair market value on the date of death, real estate included, not what the owner paid.

Is an inherited Colorado house taxed when the heirs sell?

Possibly, but only on gain above the heir's basis. The IRS says in Topic 703 that basis for property acquired by gift or inheritance is not simply cost, and points to Publication 551 for the rules. Gain is the sale price minus selling costs minus that basis.

The home sale exclusion may help. IRS Topic 701 allows up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return, if the seller owned and lived in the home at least 24 of the last 60 months. An heir who never lived in the house will not pass the use test, so any gain is taxable. Colorado's tax starts from federal taxable income, so the federal result carries over.

  • Get a date of death value for the house, such as an appraisal, before listing.
  • Keep estate records showing what the heirs received.
  • Report the sale even if no tax is due when you receive Form 1099-S.

What withholding applies when a nonresident heir sells Colorado property?

When a nonresident sells Colorado real property, the Department of Revenue says income tax is generally withheld from the proceeds. The title company or closing agent holds back the lesser of 2% of the sales price of the seller's interest or the seller's net proceeds, and remits it with form DR 1079. The details are in the Department of Revenue's nonresident guidance.

Estates have their own version. A fiduciary of an estate or trust with a nonresident beneficiary who receives net income from Colorado real or tangible personal property must withhold income tax from the distribution, using form DR 0104BEP. The rate is the applicable income tax rate for the year times the beneficiary's net Colorado property income.

These amounts are prepayments. Nonresidents can claim them on a Colorado return and get a refund if they exceed the tax owed.

How does Colorado compare with other states on death taxes?

Colorado is not among the states that tax estates or inheritances. In 2023 the handbook counted 11 states plus Washington, D.C. with an estate tax and six states with an inheritance tax, noting that Maryland has both.

An out of state heir may live in one of those states. If so, their home state rules, not Colorado's, decide whether they owe tax on money they receive from the estate. Ask the estate attorney which rules apply.

The state does not set exemptions of its own. The handbook says no state exemptions are allowed, because the tax had been tied to the federal credit.

What is the unified credit and why does it matter here?

The unified credit is the reason most families never see a federal estate tax bill. The Colorado handbook explains that it applies to both the federal gift tax and the estate tax, which are integrated into one system, and that the amount is adjusted for inflation each year. For a person who died in 2023 it allowed gifts and bequests up to $12.92 million without gift or estate tax.

The handbook also points out that eliminating the state credit did not reduce the total estate tax paid. It moved the revenue from Colorado to the federal government.

Gifts made during life count too. The IRS says the value of lifetime taxable gifts, beginning with 1977, is added back to the net estate before the tax is computed.

Where in Colorado are the houses?

Colorado is large and varied, so the estate house could be anywhere. Wikipedia lists 6,012,561 residents in 2025 and El Paso as the largest county, with Denver as the capital and largest city. The Front Range holds the main population centers, the Western Slope has Grand Junction, Durango and Montrose, and the Eastern Plains are semi-arid prairie.

What do sellers of inherited houses in Colorado usually face?

The common problems are distance, condition and timing. Colorado has 64 counties spread from the Front Range to the Western Slope and the Eastern Plains, and an heir may live a long way from the house. According to Wikipedia, Colorado is divided into 23 judicial districts, so court contact for an estate depends on where the decedent lived.

  • Heirs who live elsewhere must handle keys, utilities and insurance remotely.
  • Houses often need cleanout before a buyer's lender will lend.
  • Several heirs have to agree on one buyer and one price.
  • Hail and wildfire damage are real risks in many parts of the state, per Wikipedia.

A cash purchase as-is can shorten the process. We buy houses in Colorado in their current condition, including estate properties.

Is there an estate tax in Colorado?

No. Colorado collects no estate tax on deaths after December 31, 2004, and no filing is required, according to the state Legislative Council Staff.

Does Colorado have an inheritance tax?

No. An inheritance tax enacted in 1927 was replaced by an estate tax in 1980, and that tax is no longer collected.

When does the federal estate tax apply to a Colorado resident?

A federal return is required when the gross estate plus certain gifts exceeds the yearly threshold, which the IRS lists as $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.

Do heirs pay tax when they sell an inherited Colorado house?

Only on gain above their basis, and the home sale exclusion may reduce it if they lived in the house. Basis for inherited property follows IRS Publication 551.

Is money withheld when a nonresident sells a Colorado house?

Yes. The closing agent generally withholds the lesser of 2 percent of the sales price or the net proceeds and sends it to the Department of Revenue.

What the official sources say

  • A Notice to Terminate Tenancy is used for repeat or substantial violations. (Residential Evictions | Colorado Judicial Branch; source)
  • If the court orders a tenant out, they are usually given 48 hours; then the plaintiff may file a Writ of Restitution (JDF 109) and the Sheriff removes the tenant. (Residential Evictions | Colorado Judicial Branch; source)

How does a Colorado eviction start?

A Colorado eviction starts with a written notice from the landlord, not with a court filing. The court case can only be filed after the notice period has run out, so the clock matters before anyone sees a judge.

The Colorado Judicial Branch lists three pre-filing notices on its residential eviction page. Which one a landlord uses depends on why the tenant is being asked to leave.

NoticeCourt formTypical useTime given
Demand for ComplianceJDF 99 AFix a lease violation or pay past-due rent3 to 30 days, set by the rental agreement
Notice to Terminate TenancyJDF 99 BRepeated or substantial violations, criminal behavior, some non-renewals1 to 91 days, set by the agreement
Notice of No-Fault EvictionJDF 99 CDemolition, repairs, owner use, sale, declined new lease, late payment historyAt least 90 days

Every notice has to be in the tenant's primary language. A notice in the wrong language is one of the easier ways for a landlord to lose time.

What does the statute say about the standard notice length?

For most residential tenants the statute sets a ten-day period. Under C.R.S. 13-40-104, that applies when a tenant holds over after unpaid rent, after breaking a material lease condition, or after conduct that disturbs others or damages the property.

The statute shortens the period in one case. An exempt residential agreement, meaning a single-family lease from a landlord who owns five or fewer such homes and says so in the agreement, can use five days. Nonresidential and employer-provided housing agreements get three days. You can read the full text on Justia.

The same section lists other situations that count as unlawful detention, and a few of them matter to anyone selling a house:

  • A tenant who stays after a foreclosure sale under a power of sale, once title is perfected and the buyer demands possession.
  • A person who refuses to leave property after the buyer under a court judgment makes a demand, once the redemption period is over.
  • An heir or devisee who will not leave property that a personal representative has sold, after a demand.
  • A contract buyer who fails to perform and keeps possession after a demand.

The heir and devisee item matters for inherited houses: a relative who will not leave after the personal representative sells the property can face an eviction case.

What happens after the notice period ends?

Once the notice period expires, the landlord can file in the county where the property sits. The filing package is the Complaint (JDF 101), the Summons (JDF 102) and a copy of the notice that was posted or delivered.

The person filing has to be the person in interest, which means the owner or the landlord named as lessor in the lease. A property manager may need to show proof of authority.

Colorado also requires mediation in most residential cases. Under C.R.S. 13-40-110, a complaint is started on the standard form, and skipping the mediation step where it applies is an affirmative defense that can lead to dismissal without prejudice. The statute carves out certain tenants and landlords, so check the current rule before relying on it.

A dismissal without prejudice means the landlord can start over, which adds time to any plan to sell.

How is the tenant served, and how fast does the case move?

Service has to be complete at least seven days before the hearing date printed on the summons. The court page describes two routes.

  • Personal service. Handed over by the sheriff in the county where the tenant lives or works, a private process server, or an adult who is not part of the case. An Affidavit of Service (JDF 98) is needed for each defendant.
  • Posting and mailing. If personal service fails, the papers can be posted on the main door of the dwelling, and the summons, complaint and answer form must be mailed by the day after filing. The Certificate of Mailing on JDF 102 goes back to the court.

The difference has money attached. Personal service is required if the landlord wants a money judgment for back rent. Posting and mailing supports possession only.

A tenant who wants to contest the case files a written answer on JDF 103. If the tenant does not answer or show up, the court can enter a default judgment.

What defenses can a tenant raise?

The best known defense is unlivable conditions, found in C.R.S. 38-12-503. It applies to a nonpayment case when the home was unfit to live in and the tenant gave written notice on JDF 104. The landlord then has five days to repair unless the tenant caused the problem.

That defense comes with a cost. The tenant must pay the rent due into the court registry, minus allowed expenses, and a tenant who does not pay the full amount at filing is in default.

Attorney fees follow a simple rule. The losing side pays only if the lease says so. If the lease is silent, each side bears its own fees.

For a seller, the practical point is that an unrepaired house can turn a routine nonpayment case into a contested one. Dated repair requests and records of what was fixed become relevant to that defense.

What happens if the tenant stays after a judgment?

After a court orders the tenant out, the tenant usually has 48 hours to leave. If the tenant is still there, the plaintiff fills out a Writ of Restitution (JDF 109) and returns it to the court for the judge's signature.

Once signed, the plaintiff contacts the sheriff to schedule the removal. The sheriff charges a fee for serving the writ.

If you are weighing a sale, add up the likely timeline before choosing a path:

  • Notice period (3 to 30 days for a demand, up to 91 for a termination, 90 or more for no-fault).
  • Time to file and serve, with at least seven days before the hearing.
  • Hearing, judgment and the 48-hour window.
  • Writ, sheriff scheduling and removal.

Can I evict a tenant because I want to sell?

Yes, but only through the no-fault route with a long notice. The JDF 99 C form lists the reason as "The Landlord intends to stop renting and sell the home," under C.R.S. 38-12-1303(3)(d).

The move-out date has to fall after the lease term ends and be at least 90 days after the notice is served. If the landlord or the landlord's spouse is on active U.S. military duty, the minimum drops to 45 days. Service is by leaving a copy with the tenant or posting it in a conspicuous place at the home.

The state's JDF 99 C form shows who is not covered:

  • Tenants who have lived in the home less than a year, or whom the landlord does not know to be a tenant.
  • Tenants of a resident landlord who lives in or next to a single-family home, duplex or triplex.
  • Employer-provided housing, mobile home spaces and short-term rentals.

The form sets no deadline for listing or closing after the notice. It also says nothing about a new owner. A buyer who plans to take the house with tenants should ask for the lease and any notices before closing.

Does an eviction have to finish before a house can be sold?

No. A rented or occupied house can be sold as is, and the sale contract decides who deals with the occupants. The eviction process only controls how a tenant can be removed, not whether the owner can sell.

Owners who sell to a cash buyer often choose a closing date that fits the notice or court timeline, so the buyer takes the house after the occupant has gone, or takes it with the tenant in place. The right choice depends on the lease, the notice already served and the stage of any court case.

The deed that transfers the house is recorded with the county clerk and recorder, who collects the documentary fee. Under C.R.S. 39-13-102, that fee is one cent for each $100 of consideration, and no fee is due when the consideration is $500 or less.

None of this replaces advice from a Colorado attorney if a case is already filed. If you would like to talk through a sale while a tenant is still in the house, we can look at the lease and the dates with you.

More questions about Colorado Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How many days does a Colorado landlord have to give for a standard eviction notice?

The standard residential period under C.R.S. 13-40-104 is ten days. Five days applies to exempt single-family leases from landlords who own five or fewer such homes, and three days applies to nonresidential and employer-provided housing.

How long does a tenant have to move out after the judge rules?

Usually 48 hours. If the tenant stays, the landlord files a Writ of Restitution (JDF 109) and the sheriff schedules the removal.

Can I sell my house while the tenant is still living in it?

Yes. A sale does not require the home to be empty. The contract decides whether the buyer takes the house with the tenant or after the tenant has left.

How much notice does a landlord need to give if the house is being sold?

At least 90 days after service, and the move-out date must fall after the lease term ends. The date can be as short as 45 days if the landlord or spouse is on active military duty.

Can the landlord keep a tenant's rent money if the tenant answers the case?

A tenant who raises the unlivable conditions defense has to pay the rent due into the court registry, less allowed expenses. The court then decides the case.

Do I need to serve the tenant personally to get back rent?

Yes. Personal service is required to seek a money judgment. Posting and mailing supports possession only.

Where is an eviction case filed?

In the county where the property is located, by the owner or the landlord named as lessor in the lease.

  • Arapahoe County adds a documentary fee of $0.10 per $1,000 consideration on documents conveying title. (Recording Fees | Arapahoe County; source)

What is a quitclaim deed in Colorado?

A Colorado quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the signer holds in a property, with no promise that the title is good. Under C.R.S. 38-30-113, the deed carries no warranty words, uses "quitclaim(s)" in place of "convey(s)", and passes no after-acquired title.

That last point is easy to miss. If the grantor later obtains a better interest in the same property, a quitclaim does not hand that interest to the grantee. A bargain and sale deed does, which is one of the real differences between the forms.

The statute also says a properly executed deed in one of the listed forms conveys the property, and the form does not reduce the fee simple estate unless the deed reserves something.

How does a quitclaim differ from other Colorado deeds?

The four statutory forms differ mainly in how much the grantor promises. Here is how C.R.S. 38-30-113 sets them out.

  • Warranty deed: includes the words "and warrant(s) the title to the same" and covers the property's whole history.
  • Special warranty deed: warrants the title only against people claiming under the grantor, so the promise covers the grantor's period of ownership.
  • Bargain and sale deed: no warranty, but it does pass after-acquired title.
  • Quitclaim deed: no warranty and no after-acquired title.

A warranty or special warranty deed may be made "subject to statutory exceptions." Those exceptions are real estate taxes for the year of conveyance and later years not yet due, matters disclosed by a survey or inspection, and matters recorded with the county clerk and recorder. A quitclaim makes none of these promises in the first place.

What does a Colorado quitclaim deed need to include?

The deed has to identify the property precisely, name the right people and be acknowledged before a notary. El Paso County's recording flyer tells filers to include the full legal description and to make sure it mirrors the county's records.

  • Owners: when adding someone to a title, list everyone who needs to be on it, not only the new person.
  • Legal description: copy it from the county's records, not from a street address.
  • Notary: the notary must complete the entire notarial section.
  • Grantee address: C.R.S. 38-35-109 says deeds dated after January 1, 1977 must include the grantee's legal address, and a deed without it is returned for recording.

The deed statute takes a looser line, saying that leaving out an address or county of residence does not invalidate the deed. The two statutes cover different points, validity in one case and recordability in the other, so supply the address anyway. Margins matter too. Gunnison County cites C.R.S. 30-10-406 for a top margin of at least one inch and at least half an inch on the other sides, and a clerk may refuse a document that does not conform.

Where is a Colorado quitclaim deed recorded?

It is recorded with the clerk and recorder of the county where the land lies. C.R.S. 38-35-109 says deeds and court orders affecting title are recorded with the county clerk and recorder where the land is located, and treats filing and recording as the same thing.

Colorado has 64 counties, so a house in Colorado Springs goes to El Paso County and a cabin in Gunnison County goes there, whichever county the owners live in. El Paso's Recording Department lists a phone number of 719-520-6200 and the email recweb@elpasoco.com on its flyer.

How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in Colorado?

In El Paso County, a completed quitclaim deed records for a flat $43. The County Clerk and Recorder says the fee took effect July 1, 2025, under House Bill 24-1269, and covers every document recorded there regardless of page count.

Gunnison County's schedule also shows $43 for a standard document and $0 for a death certificate, which fits El Paso's note that death documents recorded into real estate records are free. Gunnison adds that card payments carry a vendor surcharge of at least $2.00 or 3.5%. Check your own county's schedule, since the fee is set by statute but each office publishes its own rules.

Is there a documentary fee on a Colorado deed?

Yes, when a deed conveys ownership for money. Gunnison County explains that any document conveying real property must pay the state documentary fee under C.R.S. 39-13-102, set at $0.01 per $100, which equals $0.10 per $1,000.

Transfers of under $500 are exempt. The Transfer Declaration, form TD 1000, accompanies the deed, is not recorded and is kept confidential. The recording office can tell you whether the fee applies to a particular transfer.

Why does recording a Colorado deed matter?

An unrecorded deed can lose to a later recorded one. C.R.S. 38-35-109 says an unrecorded instrument is not valid against any person with rights in the property who records first, with exceptions for the parties themselves and anyone who had notice.

The same section warns that a person who records a document they know or have reason to know is forged, groundless or invalid can owe at least $1,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees. If a family member asks you to sign a quitclaim to clear up a loan or a dispute, read the document and understand what the deed does before signing.

When does a quitclaim deed work, and when does it fall short?

A quitclaim fits transfers between people who already trust each other, such as adding a spouse or moving a house into a family arrangement. It falls short when a buyer needs a promise about the title, since the grantor gives none.

  • Works for: moving a known interest from one family member to another, and cleaning up the name on an existing title.
  • Falls short for: a sale to an outside buyer who expects title warranties, or any case where the title history is unclear.
  • Does not fix: unpaid property tax, liens or a loan tied to the property. Ask the lender, the title company or an attorney.

When heirs inherit a house and one sibling wants out, a quitclaim from that sibling to the others can move the interest. If the estate still has to be opened first, however, the title may not belong to the signer yet. Colorado's probate rules decide who can sign for an estate, and our Colorado probate guide covers that side.

Can I sell a Colorado house after using a quitclaim deed?

Yes, but the buyer's title company will look at how title reached you. A seller who received the property by quitclaim has to show that the chain of recorded deeds supports a sale.

Sellers in that position often choose a cash buyer who buys as-is, because there are fewer repairs and showings to manage while the paperwork is checked. If the contract calls for a warranty or special warranty deed, the seller makes the title promises that a quitclaim leaves out, so read the deed form before closing.

Does a Colorado quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?

No. Under C.R.S. 38-30-113, a quitclaim has no warranty words and passes no after-acquired title, so the grantor promises nothing about the title.

How much does it cost to record a deed in El Paso County, Colorado?

A completed quitclaim deed records for a flat $43 in El Paso County. That is a $40 fee, a $1 ERTB surcharge and a $2 electronic filing surcharge, effective July 1, 2025.

Does the notary have to complete the whole section?

Yes. El Paso County's recording flyer says the notary must complete the entire notarial section of the deed.

Do I pay a documentary fee on a quitclaim deed in Colorado?

Possibly. Any document conveying real property pays the state documentary fee of $0.01 per $100 under C.R.S. 39-13-102, with purchases under $500 exempt, and the TD 1000 declaration accompanies the deed.

Where do I record a Colorado quitclaim deed?

With the clerk and recorder of the county where the land is located. For Colorado Springs, that is the El Paso County Recording Department at 719-520-6200.

Colorado Transfer on Death Deed Explained FAQ

What is a transfer on death deed?

A recorded deed that names who receives the property when the owner dies. Confirm the Colorado rules with an attorney.

What is a transfer on death deed in Colorado?

Colorado calls it a beneficiary deed. It is a deed that names who receives a house when the owner dies, and under C.R.S. 15-15-401 it is subject to revocation by the owner and says the conveyance takes effect on the owner's death.

The person who signs is the owner, and the person named is the grantee-beneficiary. A successor grantee-beneficiary can also be named to take if the first choice does not survive the owner. The rules sit in Part 4 of Article 15 of the Colorado Probate Code, sections 15-15-401 through 15-15-415.

Many people look for a Colorado transfer on death deed because they want a house to skip probate. The statute says a beneficiary deed is not a will, and it cannot be thrown out for failing the formalities that apply to wills (15-15-412).

Which Colorado statute sections cover beneficiary deeds?

Part 4 of Article 15 holds the whole set of rules, and each section answers one question. The table lists the ones we read on the Justia copy of the Colorado statutes.

SectionTopic
15-15-401Definitions of beneficiary deed, owner and grantee-beneficiary
15-15-402Recording before death, no consideration, owner keeps control
15-15-403Medicaid eligibility
15-15-404Form of the deed and recording before death
15-15-405Revoking a beneficiary deed
15-15-406Acknowledgment
15-15-407Vesting of title and later claims
15-15-408Joint tenants
15-15-410Protection for a buyer from the grantee-beneficiary
15-15-411Time limits on claims
15-15-412Not a testamentary disposition

Justia warns that its copy may not be the newest version, so a final check against the official Colorado statutes is worth the few minutes.

What has to happen before the owner dies?

The deed must be recorded during the owner's lifetime with the county clerk and recorder where the house sits. Section 15-15-404 puts it in capital letters on the sample form: the deed must be recorded before the grantor's death to be effective.

A few other points from the statute:

  • No payment from the beneficiary is required, because the section says no consideration is needed.
  • The beneficiary does not have to sign, agree or be told before the owner dies, though the beneficiary may still disclaim the property.
  • The deed has to meet the notarization and acknowledgment rules in 15-15-406, which point to C.R.S. 38-35-109 and 38-35-101.
  • Unless the owner says otherwise, the deed carries no title warranties and works like a bargain and sale deed.

The sample form also tells the assessor and treasurer that the beneficiary's address is only for identification. Tax notices keep going to the owner while the owner is alive.

What does recording a beneficiary deed cost in Colorado?

Recording is a county charge, and the two county pages we opened both list a $43 fee per document. The Denver recording page and the Delta County recording page each give that figure.

Denver also asks for one-inch top margins and half-inch side margins on documents, and it says mailed documents can take 7 to 10 days while e-recording takes minutes. Other counties set their own fees and habits, so call the clerk in the county where the house sits before you mail anything.

Delta County states that death certificates and verification-of-death documents recorded in the real estate records have no fee. That matters later, when a beneficiary needs the death on record.

Can the owner still sell the house after signing the deed?

Yes. During the owner's life the beneficiary has no right, title or interest, and the owner keeps full power over the property without the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice (15-15-402).

That means a homeowner who recorded a beneficiary deed years ago can still list the house, take a cash offer, refinance or pledge it. A normal sale deed signed by the owner passes title to the buyer, and the old beneficiary deed has nothing left to transfer once the house is gone.

Sellers sometimes get stuck because family members believe the named beneficiary has to approve. The statute says the opposite while the owner is alive. If the owner has lost capacity, the question becomes who holds authority to sign, and that is a job for an attorney.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Colorado houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do you cancel or change a beneficiary deed?

The owner signs and records a written revocation before death. Under 15-15-405 it must describe the property, revoke the deed, and be recorded with the clerk and recorder in the county where the property is located.

  • The beneficiary does not need to sign or be notified.
  • A new beneficiary deed for the same property revokes all earlier ones, even if it covers only part of the owner's interest.
  • If several deeds or revocations are recorded before death, the one signed most recently controls, whatever the recording order.
  • A will cannot revoke or change a beneficiary deed that follows the statute.

The will point catches families by surprise. A will that leaves the house to one child does nothing against a recorded beneficiary deed naming another.

How do joint tenants and Medicaid affect a beneficiary deed?

A joint tenant can use a beneficiary deed, but title passes to the named person only if that joint tenant is the last surviving joint tenant (15-15-408). The deed does not break the joint tenancy.

Medicaid is the other trap. Section 15-15-403 says a person applying for or receiving medical assistance cannot qualify while holding an effective beneficiary deed where the state could assert a repayment claim, and signing one while applying makes the property a countable resource.

Section 15-15-407 adds that the beneficiary's interest is subject to the state's claims to recover medical assistance payments. Anyone near a nursing-home or Medicaid decision should get advice before recording or leaving a deed in place.

What happens when the owner dies?

Title vests in the beneficiary only at the owner's death, and the beneficiary takes the owner's interest subject to existing liens, later interests and interests the beneficiary knows about (15-15-407).

If the house carries a mortgage, the loan stays with the house. A deed of trust the owner signed does not disappear because a beneficiary deed exists.

Can a beneficiary sell the house quickly after inheriting it?

Yes, once title has vested, the beneficiary can sell like any other owner, and a buyer or lender who pays value without notice gets protection under 15-15-410.

That section says such a buyer takes the property free of the rights of interested persons in the estate, and a recorded transfer that shows the state documentary fee is prima facie evidence the transfer was for value. The beneficiary stays answerable to the estate's personal representative for duties under 15-15-103.

In practice, buyers and title companies want to see the recorded beneficiary deed, proof of death on record, and a clean payoff for any loan.

If you inherited a Colorado house through a beneficiary deed and want to talk about selling it as is, call us for a written cash offer. Decisions about debts, other heirs and Medicaid recovery belong with an attorney.

Questions to ask before you rely on a beneficiary deed

  • Is the deed recorded in the right county, and was it recorded before the owner died?
  • Was it signed and acknowledged to the standard in 15-15-406?
  • Does a later deed or revocation exist that was signed after this one?
  • Was the owner on Medicaid, or planning to apply?
  • Are there loans, tax bills or unrecorded claims on the house?

A title company can search the recorded documents for the answers to the first, third and fifth questions.

More questions about Colorado Transfer on Death Deed

Is a beneficiary deed the same as a transfer on death deed in Colorado?

Yes. Colorado statutes use the term beneficiary deed, and it does the work other states call a transfer on death deed. It conveys the owner's interest at death and is revocable while the owner lives.

Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?

No. Section 15-15-402 says the beneficiary does not need to join in, sign, consent to or be notified of the deed before the owner dies. The beneficiary may still disclaim the property.

Does a will override a beneficiary deed in Colorado?

No. Under 15-15-405, a beneficiary deed that follows the statute cannot be revoked or changed by the owner's will. Revocation takes a recorded written instrument signed before death.

Can I sell my house if I recorded a beneficiary deed?

Yes. While you are alive the beneficiary has no interest, and you keep full authority over the property under 15-15-402 without anyone else's consent.

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

The statute says anti-lapse rules do not apply to beneficiary deeds, and if one of several beneficiaries dies first with no alternate named, that share goes to the surviving beneficiaries in proportion. A named successor grantee-beneficiary can be designated, so check how the deed was written.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a beneficiary deed property?

Creditor claims against the owner are barred one year after the owner's death under 15-15-411. Other claims by heirs or devisees are barred at the earlier of three years after death or one year after the death is recorded in the county.

Colorado Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in Colorado
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Colorado Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale

What the official sources say

Selling in Colorado?

How does probate work in Colorado?

Colorado probate is a district court process in which a personal representative is appointed to collect a deceased owner's assets, pay valid debts and pass the rest to heirs or devisees. The Colorado Judicial Branch tells filers that they must pick the type of case themselves, because its Open an Estate page says the court cannot make that decision for them.

The Colorado Bar Association's public pamphlet describes the same arc: a representative is appointed, creditors are notified, assets are valued and sold or distributed, and the case closes once debts, distributions and tax returns are finished. For a family holding an inherited house, the practical point is that nobody can sign a sale contract for the estate until someone holds that authority.

The pamphlet also says a will must be lodged with the district court where the decedent lived within ten days of death, even when no administration is expected. It is a 2011 publication and warns that the law may have changed, so treat that figure as a prompt to ask the court clerk, not as the final word.

Which Colorado court handles an estate?

An estate is opened in the district court of the county where the deceased lived. If the person lived out of state, the Judicial Branch says to file in any Colorado county where they owned property, which matters for a family inheriting a cabin or rental in the mountains.

Denver is the exception to the district court rule, since the state's guidance says to file there in the Denver Probate Court. Colorado has 64 counties, and Denver and Broomfield are consolidated city-counties, so the county you start in depends on where the owner lived, not where the house sits.

Anyone who files without a lawyer is held to the same rules as an attorney, according to the self-help page. That is worth knowing before you start a formal case over a house with a mortgage and a buyer waiting.

Informal or formal probate: what is the difference?

Informal probate is reviewed by the probate registrar with no hearing, and formal probate is reviewed by the court with a chance for interested people to object before approval. The Judicial Branch lists four paths, each with its own forms.

  • With a will, informal: JDF 910, with instructions in JDF 906. No notice is required before the case is accepted.
  • With a will, formal: JDF 920, which is required if you only have a copy of the will.
  • Without a will, informal: JDF 916, with instructions in JDF 907.
  • Without a will, formal: a petition for intestacy on JDF 922.

The Bar pamphlet adds that informal cases fit a valid will or clear intestacy with no contest expected, while formal cases suit disputes, unclear wills or trouble finding heirs. When a house is the main asset and the siblings disagree about selling it, formal probate is the route the pamphlet points to, and it usually takes longer.

Does a Colorado house always go through probate?

No. Only property held in the decedent's sole name without a beneficiary designation is controlled by the will. The Bar pamphlet says jointly owned real property and assets with beneficiary designations, such as life insurance or IRAs, pass outside probate.

Even so, the same pamphlet states that all wills and intestate estates must be probated, with the level of court involvement varying. A house titled only to the person who died is the typical case that needs a personal representative before it can be sold.

The small estate affidavit is the shortcut people ask about. The Judicial Branch says it is available only when no real estate has to be transferred, and the affidavit form (JDF 999) is not filed with the court. State law at C.R.S. 15-12-1201 also requires that ten days have passed since death and that no petition to appoint a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere. If the estate owns a house outright, plan on a regular case.

What are the probate deadlines in Colorado?

The first deadlines are short. A case can be filed 120 hours after death, and the appointed representative has 30 days to notify interested persons and 90 days to prepare an inventory. The table pulls those dates together with the creditor rules from the statutes.

StepTimingSource
Earliest court filing120 hours after deathColorado Judicial Branch
Creditor opening an estateWait at least 45 daysColorado Judicial Branch
Notice of appointment to interested persons (JDF 940)Within 30 days of appointmentColorado Judicial Branch
Inventory (JDF 941)Within 90 days of appointment; given to interested persons who askColorado Judicial Branch
Published notice to creditorsThree times, once in each of three successive calendar weeksC.R.S. 15-12-801
Claims for debts that arose before deathBarred one year after death at the latestC.R.S. 15-12-803
Claims arising after deathFour months after the claim arisesC.R.S. 15-12-803

The inventory is not filed with the court, but beneficiaries who request it are entitled to a copy. Keeping it current helps when a buyer's title company asks what the estate owns.

How are creditors paid when an estate owns a house?

The personal representative gives creditors notice and pays the valid claims before distributing what is left. Under C.R.S. 15-12-801, the representative publishes notice in a newspaper in the county, and may also mail written notice to a known creditor.

A creditor who gets written notice must present a claim by the later of the date in the published notice or 60 days after the notice is mailed or delivered, and in any case within one year of death. A creditor who misses the deadline is barred. A secured lender is different, since the Justia annotations to the statute note that a secured creditor can enforce a lien by foreclosure without filing a claim. A mortgage on the inherited house does not wait on the claims period.

C.R.S. 15-12-803 also says its deadlines cannot be waived or tolled. That is one reason heirs who want a quick sale still need the representative to follow the notice steps.

Can the estate sell the house before probate closes?

Yes, once a personal representative has been appointed. The Bar pamphlet lists the power to sell, transfer or encumber real property among the representative's duties, and it says the representative must inventory real and personal assets with titling and date-of-death values.

The same pamphlet says informal and formal probates stay open at least six months. A sale can happen sooner, but the case itself will outlast the closing. Meanwhile the carrying costs continue, and in a county like El Paso, the Treasurer reports interest of 1% per month on late tax payments with no grace period.

  • Real estate taxes: the bill goes to the owner of record, and not receiving it does not excuse late payment.
  • Mortgage: the lender can proceed on its lien regardless of the creditor claims period.
  • Insurance and upkeep: someone has to pay for them while the estate is open.
  • Time spent: the pamphlet says a representative should track hours, since reasonable compensation is allowed.

A cash buyer that purchases as-is can shorten the stretch between appointment and closing, because the house does not need repairs or showings first. The representative still signs, and the sale still follows the court's rules for the estate.

What does Colorado probate cost?

The court charges a filing fee, and the Judicial Branch page does not list an amount. Filers who cannot pay can request a waiver with JDF 205 and the caption of JDF 206.

Other costs come from the estate itself: attorney fees, final expenses of the decedent and legitimate debts. The Bar pamphlet says attorneys usually bill hourly, with rates that depend on experience, difficulty and results. Selling a house adds its own closing costs, so heirs should ask for a written estimate before choosing an approach.

What problems come with inherited Colorado houses?

Inherited houses in Colorado often arrive with aging roofs and deferred maintenance, and the climate adds risk. Wikipedia's Colorado entry says hail is common in the mountains east of the Continental Divide and across the Eastern Plains, and that the May 8, 2017 Denver hailstorm was the costliest in state history.

Wildfire is the other concern for mountain and foothill properties. The same entry names the 2021 Marshall Fire as the most destructive in property loss, and says the 2020 Pine Gulch, Cameron Peak and East Troublesome fires were the three largest in state history.

Heirs who live elsewhere, own the house jointly or cannot afford a roof replacement often choose to sell as-is. The personal representative should confirm insurance is active before listing or accepting any offer.

More questions about Colorado Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I need probate to sell a house in Colorado after someone dies?

Usually yes, if the house was in the deceased person's name alone with no beneficiary designation. The Colorado Bar pamphlet says jointly owned real property passes outside probate, while sole-name property is controlled by the will or intestacy. The small estate affidavit does not cover real estate transfers, according to the Colorado Judicial Branch.

How soon can I file for probate in Colorado?

The Judicial Branch says filing can happen 120 hours (five days) after death, and the court cannot act before then. A creditor who wants to open an estate must wait at least 45 days.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a Colorado estate?

It depends on the notice. Under C.R.S. 15-12-801 and 15-12-803, a creditor who gets written notice has the later of the published period or 60 days from mailing, but no more than one year after death. Claims that arise after death must be presented within four months.

Which court do I file in for a Colorado estate?

File in the district court of the county where the person lived, or the Denver Probate Court for Denver. If the person lived out of state, file in any Colorado county where they owned property.

Can the personal representative sell the house without all heirs agreeing?

The Bar pamphlet says the personal representative has the power to sell, transfer or encumber real property. It also says a formal case may require court approval of transactions, so a dispute among heirs usually calls for a lawyer's advice before any sale.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • A capital gain subtraction exists only for farmers selling agricultural real property acquired on or after May 9, 1994 and before June 4, 2009, held at least five years. (Income Tax Topics: Colorado Agricultural Land Capital Gain Subtraction | DOR; source)
  • That subtraction is limited to the lesser of net capital gain, qualifying gain, or $100,000. (Income Tax Topics: Colorado Agricultural Land Capital Gain Subtraction | DOR; source)
Selling in Colorado?
We buy Colorado houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Colorado tax capital gains on a house sale?

Colorado has no separate capital gains tax. Gain from a home sale is folded into ordinary income, because the state starts from your federal taxable income. The Department of Revenue's Individual Income Tax Guide says Colorado income tax is based generally on federal taxable income, with certain additions and subtractions.

The statute sets a single rate. C.R.S. 39-22-104 imposes 4.40 percent on federal taxable income for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2022, subject to the exceptions it names. Check the current Colorado return booklet for the rate that applies to the year you sell, since the statute refers to other provisions that can change the rate actually charged.

In practice, a seller first works out the federal result, then Colorado follows it with its own adjustments. If your federal return shows no taxable gain on the house, Colorado normally shows none either.

How does the federal home sale exclusion work for a Colorado seller?

Most owner-occupants owe nothing on the gain up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return. The IRS explains the rule in Topic 701, and Colorado inherits the result.

To qualify you must pass two tests during the five years ending on the sale date:

  • Ownership test: you owned the home at least 24 months.
  • Use test: you lived in it as a residence at least 24 months.
  • The two periods do not have to be the same 24 months.

On a joint return either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both must meet the use test. You generally cannot take the exclusion if you excluded gain on another home sale in the two years before. Military, Foreign Service and intelligence personnel on extended duty may suspend the five year period for up to 10 years.

Reporting still applies. If you receive Form 1099-S you must report the sale even when the gain is fully excludable, and you must report it when you cannot exclude all of the gain.

Which Colorado sellers are most likely to owe tax?

The sellers with a real bill are landlords, long time absentee owners, heirs who rent the house first and flippers. A house that was never your main home does not pass the use test, so the full gain is taxable.

SituationHome sale exclusionColorado treatment
Lived in the house 24 of the last 60 monthsUp to $250,000 single, $500,000 jointFollows federal taxable income
Rented out for years, never your residenceFails the use testGain is Colorado taxable income
Nonresident selling Colorado houseSame federal testColorado source income; withholding at closing
Sale paid over several yearsExclusion still availableInstallment method reported federally

Under the installment rules in IRS Topic 701, if the contract pays part of the price in a later year you report under the installment method unless you elect out, and the exclusion stays available.

What if I live outside Colorado and sell a Colorado house?

Colorado taxes the gain from real property located in the state even if you live elsewhere. The Department of Revenue's part-year resident and nonresident guidance says income from real property located in Colorado, including capital gains and losses, is Colorado source income.

The closing agent normally withholds. Whenever a nonresident sells or conveys Colorado real property, the title company or settlement provider generally holds back the lesser of two percent of the sales price of the seller's interest or the seller's net proceeds. They send it to the state with form DR 1079.

  • The withholding is a prepayment, not the final tax.
  • You claim it on your Colorado return on the line for DR 1079, not the W-2 line.
  • If it exceeds the tax due, you can claim a refund.
  • Nonresidents cannot claim the credit for tax paid to another state.

The department also mentions form DR 1083 and its instructions for more detail on this withholding. A seller who expects little or no gain should ask the title officer early how the department handles that case.

Are there Colorado subtractions that reduce a house sale gain?

Colorado allows a few narrow subtractions, and only some touch real estate. The statute lets you subtract the part of a gain that comes from having a higher Colorado basis than federal basis for the same property. It also lets you subtract income already taxed by Colorado in a prior year, so the same dollar is not taxed twice.

The one capital gain subtraction the Department of Revenue lists by name is for agricultural land, and it is limited to farmers who meet the acquisition and holding rules. A town house or a city lot does not qualify.

The Department of Revenue also lists a subtraction for wildfire mitigation measures, such as clearing defensible space around structures. It is an income deduction for work you paid for, not a break on the sale gain, but it matters if you spent money on mitigation before listing.

How do you work out your gain on a Colorado house?

Your gain is the selling price minus selling costs minus your adjusted basis. The IRS describes basis in Topic 703: it is generally what you paid, increased by improvements that add to value and decreased by items such as depreciation and casualty reimbursements.

  • Add the cost of a new roof, addition or finished basement.
  • Keep closing statements from the purchase.
  • Subtract depreciation if you ever rented the house.
  • For an inherited house, basis usually is not your parent's purchase price. IRS Publication 551 covers property received by gift or inheritance.

A short worked pattern helps. A joint couple who lived in the house for 10 years can exclude up to $500,000 of gain. If their gain is less than that, there is no federal tax, and Colorado follows. If gain is larger, only the excess is taxed, at the Colorado rate on top of the federal one.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Colorado houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When do you pay Colorado tax on a house sale?

You pay when you file your return, or sooner through estimated payments. The nonresident guidance says an individual must generally send quarterly Colorado estimated payments when the tax liability, less withholding and credits, exceeds $1,000.

Colorado return filing follows the federal rule: if you must file a federal return, or you owe Colorado tax, you file in Colorado. The department adds that a nonresident or part-year resident with Colorado source income must file when the same test is met.

This page covers state income tax only, so confirm your own numbers with a tax preparer.

What does a cash sale change about the tax picture?

A cash sale does not change how the gain is taxed. The same federal and Colorado rules apply to the price you accept, whoever the buyer is.

What a cash sale can change is timing and cost. Selling as-is can avoid repair and holding costs, and a close in days instead of months may keep you inside the two year ownership and use windows you were counting on. If a sale date near the end of the 24 month mark is in question, ask a tax professional before you sign.

More questions about Colorado Capital Gains Tax When You Sell a House

Is there a Colorado capital gains tax on selling a house?

No separate capital gains tax exists. The gain is part of Colorado taxable income, which starts from federal taxable income, and the statute sets a 4.40 percent rate for tax years from 2022.

How much of my house sale gain can I exclude?

Up to $250,000 if single, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home at least 24 months of the five years before the sale.

Do I pay Colorado tax if I live in another state?

Yes, on gain from Colorado real property. The closing agent generally withholds the lesser of 2 percent of the sales price or your net proceeds, and you reconcile on a Colorado return.

Do I report a house sale if the gain is excluded?

Yes if you receive Form 1099-S. The IRS says you must report the sale even when the gain is fully excludable.

Does Colorado have a capital gain break for farmland?

A subtraction exists for agricultural land, limited to farmers who meet the Department of Revenue's acquisition and holding rules. It does not apply to ordinary houses.
